released_bridges.name: Euclidean vector norms and normalization
released_bridges.content_boundary: Define the Euclidean norm, normalize a non-zero vector, and recognize zero-vector breakdown; exclude general normed-space theory.

learning_outcomes.text: Compute the Euclidean norm of a real vector.
Normalize a non-zero vector and verify that the result has unit Euclidean norm.
Recognize that the zero vector cannot be normalized by division by its norm.

teaching_content.text: For x = (x_1, ..., x_n)^T in R^n, the Euclidean norm is ||x||_2 = sqrt(x_1^2 + ... + x_n^2) = sqrt(x^T x).
For x != 0, compute r = ||x||_2 and set u = x/r. Then ||u||_2 = 1.
If ||x||_2 = 0, then x is the zero vector and x/||x||_2 is undefined; stop before dividing.
For x = (3, 4)^T, ||x||_2 = 5 and the normalized vector is (3/5, 4/5)^T.

sources.title: Dot Products and Orthogonality
sources.provider: University of California, Irvine / Mathematics LibreTexts
sources.evidence_locator: Fact 1 (vector length), Definition: Unit Vector, Fact 3, and Example 3: gives ||x|| = sqrt(x dot x), states x dot x = 0 iff x = 0, restricts division by ||x|| to nonzero x, proves the normalized vector has length 1, and works x = (3,4)^T to (3/5,4/5)^T.

released_bridges.name: Orthogonality, orthonormal bases, and projection coefficients
released_bridges.content_boundary: Use inner products to explain orthogonality, orthonormal bases, and scalar projection coefficients v_i^T x; exclude the spectral theorem and eigenbasis expansion because those belong to RC-003 and RC-006.

learning_outcomes.text: Test whether two real vectors are orthogonal using their inner product.
Recognize an orthonormal family from zero cross-products and unit norms.
Compute the scalar coefficient v^T x when v is a unit vector.

teaching_content.text: Real vectors u and v are orthogonal when u^T v = 0.
Vectors v_1, ..., v_k are orthonormal when v_i^T v_j = 0 for i != j and ||v_i||_2 = 1.
For a unit vector v, calculate v^T x to obtain the scalar coefficient of x in the v direction.
For v = (1, 0)^T and x = (3, 4)^T, v^T x = 3.

sources.title: ZoomNotes for Linear Algebra
sources.evidence_locator: Section 4.1, p. 30 defines orthogonality by x^T y = 0; Section 4.4, p. 33 characterizes orthogonal columns q_i by q_i^T q_i = 1 and q_i^T q_j = 0.

sources.title: Projections onto Subspaces: Lecture Summary
sources.evidence_locator: Projections section, p. 1: derives the scalar coefficient as a^T b/(a^T a); when a is a unit vector, a^T a = 1 and the coefficient reduces to a^T b. BC-04 is direct substitution into this unit-vector case.

released_bridges.name: Inner products and quadratic forms
released_bridges.content_boundary: Compute x^T A x, x^T x, and compatible scalar-vector expressions used by the Rayleigh quotient and residual; exclude general quadratic-form classification.

learning_outcomes.text: Compute x^T y and identify the scalar result.
Compute x^T A x by forming Ax and then taking the inner product with x.
Relate x^T x to the squared Euclidean norm without classifying general quadratic forms.

teaching_content.text: For real vectors x and y of the same length, x^T y is the dot product and is the scalar sum of componentwise products.
To compute x^T A x, first compute y = Ax and then compute the scalar x^T y. Check that A is square and compatible with x.
The special case x^T x equals ||x||_2^2 and is non-negative.
